column4: The danger-prayer instructions place one troop in prayer with the Prophet, then bring forward another troop that has not yet prayed; صَلَاة is enacted as ordered companies following their leader.
The change of direction reveals who follows the Messenger and who turns back on his heels, a precise leader-and-follower test with reversal built into the bodily image.
Joseph's brothers confess that God preferred him over them; the preference root returns within the story whose brothers earlier said they had gone racing in 12:17.
Between the immediate seeker of 17:18 and the higher final ranks of 17:21, this ayah says both groups receive an extension of the Lord's gift, distinguishing present provision from final placement.
Worldly life is play and diversion, while the later abode is described as the true life; the contrast sharply separates apparent early animation from lasting life.
Everything perishes except God's face, a direct formulation of what exhausts its course and what alone remains.
One class asks only for a worldly share and consequently has no share in the hereafter, making exclusive desire for the first stage determine the loss of the later one.
The next class asks for good in both the world and the hereafter, establishing a boundary against reading the section's comparison as abandonment of every worldly good.
Whoever wants worldly reward is reminded that both worldly and later reward are with God, relocating control of both stages from the chooser to their Lord.
Worldly luxury is reduced to the enjoyment of the near life, while the hereafter with the Lord belongs to the God-conscious.
The Prophet's wives are explicitly offered worldly life and its adornment as one possible choice.
Against 33:28's worldly option, choosing God, His Messenger, and the later abode leads to the prepared great reward.
The near life is adorned for rejecters who mock believers, but the God-conscious will be above them on resurrection day; the final height reverses the visible worldly rank.
After the prayer of 62:9, believers disperse, seek God's bounty, and continue remembering Him; it marks the ordered return to provision after trade was set aside.
God desires ease for people and does not desire hardship, stating the moral polarity behind being eased toward the easy course.
The promise that ease is with hardship gives a direct repeated formulation of divine ease without turning it into mere speed.
The immediate repetition that ease is with hardship reinforces 94:5 as a sustained promise rather than a passing first appearance.
God will make ease after hardship, explicitly arranging hardship and ease as successive stages.
God has made the Quran easy for remembrance; the ayah closely joins divine easing to the remembering stance developed in the section.
The same declaration that the Quran was made easy for remembrance recurs after a second warning, so this repeated occurrence has its own contextual force.
A third narrative cycle again ends by making the Quran easy for remembrance, preserving the surah's deliberate refrain.
The refrain that the Quran was made easy for remembrance returns after Lot's people, completing the repeated formulation rather than merely echoing one occurrence.
The distance becomes two bow-lengths or nearer, completing 53:8's act of drawing near with an explicit spatial measure.
What is earlier and what is later of the Prophet's burden are expressed with forms of advancing and delaying, turning temporal extent into front-and-back position.
Whatever good people send forward for themselves they will find with God, making present action an advance deposit at the later destination.
The people of the garden are told to enjoy what they sent ahead in bygone days, showing the later benefit of capacity conserved and forwarded during the first stage.
A man comes running from the farthest edge of the city, a second Qur'anic scene in which purposeful speed begins at the remote boundary.
Pharaoh's force pursues Moses' company at sunrise, clearly staging one moving group behind another.
The two companies see one another and Moses' followers fear they will be caught, supplying the closing distance in the pursuit of 26:60.
Moses answers that his Lord will guide him, identifying true guidance at the head of the pursued company.
The sea is struck open into a dry route and each parted side rises like a mountain, giving the guided train of 26:60-62 its path through water.
At the trumpet people rush from their graves toward their Lord, relocating the decisive mass movement to the later life.
People emerge swiftly from the split earth for the gathering, another concrete afterlife race whose finish is God's summons.
People hurry toward the Caller with humbled eyes, making the resurrection's movement an urgent procession rather than the preferred near-life race.
After the destroyed people pass, no remaining one can be seen; the negative remnant supplies a concrete boundary to the positive endurance claimed by أَبْقَىٰ.
The later abode is assigned to those who do not seek worldly elevation or corruption, reversing the assumption that being high in the first stage secures the last.
The command to glorify before sunrise and before sunset places praise at two ordered points of the daily course.
Night glorification and praise after prostration continue 50:39's sequence through the remaining positions of the day.
Those who pray are excepted from the anxious, hoarding human type, giving prayer a concrete contrary course.
The praying group is constant in its prayer, joining ṣalāh to endurance rather than a brief early burst.
